subsections.subsection_title: What the OSCE station may say

blocks.text: Common scenarios include:
A 65-year-old woman presents with a vaginal bulge. Take a focused history and outline management.
Perform a pelvic examination on a woman with suspected uterine prolapse.
A clinical photograph shows a bulge through the vaginal opening. Identify the likely diagnosis and explain your findings.
A woman reports a vaginal mass associated with difficulty passing urine. Assess and manage her.
Counsel a patient with symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse about conservative and surgical treatment.
A woman has recurrent prolapse after previous pelvic floor surgery. Discuss your approach.
Explain the difference between cystocele, rectocele and uterine prolapse.

Good morning. My name is Dr. … I understand that you have noticed a vaginal bulge or a sensation of something coming down. I would like to ask about your symptoms, bladder and bowel function, and how this affects your daily activities. I would then explain the examination and discuss the available treatment options. Because this is an intimate examination, I will ensure your privacy and offer a chaperone. Is that alright with you?
Before examination:
Confirm identity and obtain informed consent.
Offer a trained chaperone.
Ask about pain, urinary retention and bleeding.
Explain that you may need to examine the patient while she strains or coughs.
Ensure privacy, appropriate exposure and adequate lighting.
Position the patient comfortably, usually in the dorsal lithotomy position.
Ask the patient to empty her bladder before the examination if clinically appropriate, and document whether the examination was performed with an empty or full bladder when relevant.
Explain each step and allow the patient to stop at any time.
If there is acute urinary retention, significant bleeding or a suspected obstructed prolapse, prioritise urgent assessment.
The main support structures include:
Levator ani muscles: provide major muscular support to the pelvic organs.
Endopelvic fascia and connective tissue: support the vaginal walls and pelvic organs.
Uterosacral and cardinal ligaments: contribute to uterine and apical support.
Perineal body: contributes to support of the posterior vaginal wall and pelvic floor.
Vaginal walls: provide support for the bladder, urethra and rectum.
Prolapse may involve one or more compartments.

rows: Peritoneal sac, sometimes containing small bowel, descends into the upper vagina

blocks.text: Important: A vaginal bulge may involve several compartments simultaneously. Do not assume that all prolapse is uterine prolapse.
The bladder bulges into the anterior vaginal wall due to loss of supporting tissue.
Symptoms may include:
Vaginal bulge or pressure.
Urinary frequency or urgency.
Stress urinary incontinence.
Difficulty emptying the bladder.
A sensation of incomplete bladder emptying.
Needing to reduce the bulge manually to urinate in some cases.
A urethral component may coexist, so urinary symptoms are not always explained by a cystocele alone.
The uterus and cervix descend into the vagina and, in more severe cases, may protrude through the vaginal opening.
Symptoms can include:
A vaginal bulge.
Pelvic heaviness or dragging discomfort.
Low back discomfort in some patients.
Difficulty with intercourse.
Urinary or bowel symptoms.
Vaginal discharge, ulceration or bleeding if exposed tissue becomes irritated.
Vault prolapse occurs when the vaginal apex descends after hysterectomy. There is no uterus or cervix to prolapse in a patient who has undergone total hysterectomy.
The rectum bulges into the posterior vaginal wall.
Symptoms may include:
A vaginal bulge.
Constipation or difficulty evacuating stool.
A feeling of incomplete bowel emptying.
Needing to press against the vagina or perineum to assist defecation, known as splinting.
Pelvic pressure.
Enterocele is a herniation of a peritoneal sac, sometimes containing small bowel, into the upper vagina. It is particularly relevant in apical or post-hysterectomy prolapse.

subsections.subsection_title: Risk factors for pelvic organ prolapse

blocks.text: The main risk factors include:
Increasing age and menopause.
Vaginal childbirth, especially multiple births or instrumental delivery.
Pelvic floor injury during childbirth.
Previous pelvic floor or prolapse surgery.
Obesity.
Chronic constipation and repeated straining.
Chronic cough and conditions associated with increased intra-abdominal pressure.
Connective tissue disorders or an inherited predisposition.
Heavy physical work or repeated heavy lifting may contribute in some women.
OSCE point: Prolapse is multifactorial. Do not imply that a woman has developed prolapse because of one childbirth, sexual activity or personal failure.
Use a structured approach covering the bulge, urinary symptoms, bowel symptoms, sexual function and impact on quality of life.

content_groups.group_title: A. History of the presenting complaint

blocks.text: Ask:
When did you first notice the bulge?
Is it always present or does it come and go?
Does it worsen after standing, walking, lifting or straining?
Does it improve when you lie down?
Can you feel or see tissue coming through the vaginal opening?
Is there a sensation of heaviness, dragging or pressure?
Is there pain or discomfort?
Have the symptoms worsened over time?
Have you tried pushing the bulge back inside?
Does it interfere with walking, work or daily activities?
A bulge that worsens on straining and improves when lying down is suggestive of prolapse, although examination is needed to establish the type and severity.
Ask specifically about:
Frequency and urgency.
Urge incontinence.
Leakage on coughing, sneezing or lifting.
Difficulty initiating urination.
Weak stream or straining to pass urine.
Incomplete bladder emptying.
Needing to reduce the bulge manually to urinate.
Recurrent urinary tract infections.
Haematuria.
Episodes of inability to pass urine.
These questions are important because prolapse can coexist with bladder dysfunction or urinary incontinence.
Ask about:
Constipation.
Straining during defecation.
Incomplete bowel emptying.
Difficulty evacuating stool.
Vaginal or perineal splinting.
Faecal urgency or incontinence.
Rectal bleeding or other concerning bowel symptoms.
Do not assume that every bowel symptom is caused by prolapse; investigate other causes when indicated.
Ask about:
Number of pregnancies and births.
Vaginal versus caesarean delivery.
Instrumental deliveries and significant perineal tears.
Previous pelvic floor surgery or hysterectomy.
Menopausal status and symptoms of vaginal dryness.
Vaginal bleeding or abnormal discharge.
Sexual activity, dyspareunia and concerns about sexual function.
Previous prolapse treatment or pessary use.
Ask about:
Chronic cough, constipation and obesity.
Connective tissue disorders.
Regular medications.
Physical activities and lifting requirements.
Smoking history where relevant.
The patient's priorities, concerns and treatment preferences.
High-yield question: “How much does this problem affect your daily life?” The degree of anatomical prolapse does not always correlate with the severity of symptoms.

subsections.subsection_title: Physical examination of pelvic organ prolapse

blocks.text: The examination must identify the affected compartment, assess the extent of descent and look for associated abnormalities.
Assess:
General condition and mobility.
Body mass index if relevant.
Abdominal distension, masses or tenderness.
A palpable bladder if urinary retention is suspected.
Signs of chronic cough or other contributing conditions when relevant.
With consent and a chaperone offered, inspect the vulva and vaginal opening.
Look for:
Protruding vaginal tissue.
The position of the cervix, if present.
Vaginal dryness or atrophy.
Pressure sores, ulceration or bleeding.
Discharge or evidence of infection.
Scarring from previous childbirth or surgery.
Ask the patient to cough or perform a Valsalva manoeuvre (bear down as if passing stool) to demonstrate the prolapse.
If the prolapse is not evident while lying down, a standing examination may be useful if safe and acceptable to the patient.
Use an appropriate speculum blade to support or retract the posterior vaginal wall, allowing you to inspect the anterior compartment.
Ask the patient to strain and observe whether the anterior vaginal wall descends.
Findings may suggest a cystocele or other anterior compartment defect.
Support the anterior vaginal wall while inspecting the posterior vaginal wall.
Ask the patient to strain.
Look for a posterior bulge suggesting rectocele or enterocele. Correlate with bowel symptoms, particularly splinting and incomplete evacuation.
Identify the cervix and its position where the uterus is present. Assess how far it descends with straining.
In a patient who has undergone hysterectomy, assess the vaginal apex for vault prolapse.
A bimanual examination may help assess the uterus, pelvic masses or other pathology when clinically indicated.
If tissue protrudes beyond the vaginal opening, inspect for:
Dryness and irritation.
Ulceration or pressure injury.
Bleeding.
Infection or abnormal discharge.
Suspicious lesions.
Persistent ulceration or a suspicious lesion needs further assessment rather than being automatically attributed to friction from prolapse.
Explain that the examination is complete.
Help the patient get comfortable and cover themselves.
Discuss findings sensitively.
Explain that further tests may be needed, especially if urinary symptoms are present.
Document consent, chaperone details and findings according to local policy.
A rectal examination is not routine for every patient. It may be indicated when posterior compartment pathology or another anorectal condition requires further assessment.

subsections.subsection_title: Grading and staging of pelvic organ prolapse

blocks.text: Some examinations use a simplified first-to-fourth-degree description of uterine prolapse.

rows: Cervix descends into the vagina but remains above the vaginal opening
Cervix descends to or approximately at the vaginal opening
Cervix or uterus protrudes beyond the vaginal opening, but the prolapse is not completely externalised
Complete or near-complete eversion of the vagina, often termed procidentia

blocks.text: This traditional system is a useful examination framework, but terminology and definitions can vary. It mainly describes uterine descent and does not adequately stage every compartment.
The Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) system provides a standardised anatomical assessment. Measurements are recorded in centimetres relative to the hymen during maximal straining.

rows: No prolapse demonstrated using POP-Q criteria.
The most distal prolapse point remains more than 1 cm above the hymen.
The most distal point is within 1 cm above or below the hymen.
The most distal point extends more than 1 cm beyond the hymen, but complete or near-complete vaginal eversion has not occurred.
Complete or near-complete eversion of the vagina.

blocks.text: POP-Q staging uses defined anatomical reference points and measurements. The full system includes anterior, posterior and apical measurements, not simply the position of the cervix.

content_groups.group_title: C. How to report the stage in an OSCE

blocks.text: For example:

“There is an anterior vaginal wall prolapse that descends to approximately the hymenal plane on maximal straining. The findings are consistent with anterior compartment prolapse, clinically around POP-Q stage II, subject to formal measurements.”
Do not assign a precise POP-Q stage without sufficient anatomical information.
Pelvic organ prolapse is primarily a clinical diagnosis. Investigations are guided by symptoms, examination findings and the planned treatment.

rows: Urinary symptoms, suspected UTI or haematuria
Difficulty emptying the bladder, retention or suspected obstruction
Assessment for stress urinary incontinence when appropriate
Selected patients with complex urinary symptoms or when results may change management
Suspected pelvic mass or another indication; not routine for uncomplicated prolapse
Renal function tests and renal imaging
Selected patients with significant retention, recurrent complications or suspected upper urinary tract effects
According to age, screening history and local programme—not because prolapse itself requires screening
Persistent ulceration, an atypical mass or concern about malignancy

blocks.text: Exam point: Routine imaging is not required to diagnose uncomplicated pelvic organ prolapse. Do not order urodynamic testing for every patient; use it when the clinical situation warrants it.
Management depends on symptom severity, compartment involved, urinary and bowel function, overall health, sexual activity and patient preference.
The most important counselling principle is that treatment is guided by symptoms and the patient's goals, not simply by the stage of prolapse.
Appropriate for women with mild symptoms, those who prefer to avoid surgery, and many patients with more significant symptoms who wish to try non-surgical options.
Address constipation with appropriate dietary fibre, fluids and treatment where indicated.
Manage chronic cough.
Consider weight management where relevant.
Discuss modifying activities that consistently worsen symptoms.
Encourage smoking cessation when appropriate.
Teach correct contraction of the pelvic floor muscles.
Recommend supervised pelvic floor muscle training, commonly for at least 16 weeks or approximately 3–6 months.
A trained pelvic floor physiotherapist can assess technique and progress.
Explain that training may improve symptoms and support, particularly in mild prolapse, but may not reverse advanced anatomical prolapse.
A vaginal pessary is a removable device placed in the vagina to support the prolapsed organs.
Common types include:
Ring pessary, sometimes with support.
Gellhorn pessary.
Other space-occupying pessaries for selected cases.
Counselling should cover:
The purpose and expected symptom relief.
Fitting and checking for comfort.
Possible discharge, spotting, irritation or expulsion.
The need for regular follow-up and removal or cleaning according to the pessary type and local protocol.
The importance of reporting pain, difficulty passing urine, bleeding or foul-smelling discharge.

Vaginal oestrogen may be considered for selected postmenopausal patients with genitourinary symptoms or atrophic vaginal tissue, particularly when a pessary is used, provided it is clinically appropriate.
Consider surgery when symptoms remain troublesome despite conservative treatment, the patient prefers surgery after informed counselling, or complications require intervention.
Possible procedures include:

rows: Posterior vaginal wall repair (posterior colporrhaphy), with perineal repair where indicated
Uterus-preserving procedures such as selected hysteropexy techniques, or hysterectomy with appropriate apical support
Vaginal or abdominal apical suspension procedures, including sacrocolpopexy in selected patients
Advanced prolapse in selected patients who do not desire future vaginal intercourse
Obliterative surgery, such as colpocleisis, after detailed counselling

blocks.text: The choice depends on the patient's anatomy, age, general health, prior surgery, desire to retain the uterus, sexual function and informed preferences.
Counselling should include potential benefits, recurrence, urinary symptoms, bleeding, infection, injury to surrounding organs, dyspareunia and other procedure-specific risks.
Mesh procedures have specific risks and regulatory considerations. Discuss only the procedures appropriate to the patient and the local service, including relevant alternatives.

content_groups.group_title: C. Management of associated urinary symptoms

blocks.text: Investigate urinary symptoms rather than assuming prolapse is the sole cause.
Treat urinary tract infection when confirmed or strongly suspected according to clinical guidance.
Assess significant residual urine or retention and manage promptly.
Consider stress incontinence and occult stress incontinence when planning prolapse surgery.
Refer for specialist evaluation when symptoms are complex or persistent.
Urgent assessment is needed for:
Acute urinary retention.
Significant bleeding from exposed tissue.
Severe pain or ulceration with suspected infection.
Tissue that is severely oedematous, compromised or irreducible.
Suspected renal complications or another acute pelvic condition.
Management may include bladder drainage, careful assessment of exposed tissue, treatment of infection when present and urgent gynaecological review.

subsections.subsection_title: How to counsel a patient about prolapse

blocks.text: A common OSCE counselling station asks you to explain the diagnosis and available options to a woman who is worried about a vaginal bulge.
A model answer:

“Your symptoms and examination suggest that one or more of the structures supported by the pelvic floor have descended, causing the bulge you can feel. This is called pelvic organ prolapse. It is common, particularly after childbirth and with increasing age, and it is not usually life-threatening.

Treatment depends on how much it bothers you and what you would like to achieve. Options include pelvic floor muscle training, measures to reduce straining and constipation, and a vaginal pessary that supports the prolapse. If these options do not help enough, or if you prefer a surgical approach, we can discuss operations designed to repair or support the affected area.

I would also like to ask about your bladder and bowel function, because these can be affected. We can then agree on a plan that fits your symptoms, health and preferences. You do not have to choose surgery simply because a prolapse is present.”
Check understanding, invite questions and use shared decision-making.

subsections.subsection_title: Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is pelvic organ prolapse?
Answer: It is descent of one or more pelvic organs into or through the vagina because of weakness or damage to the pelvic floor muscles, fascia and supporting ligaments.
Q2. What is the difference between a cystocele and a rectocele?
Answer: A cystocele is prolapse of the bladder into the anterior vaginal wall. A rectocele is bulging of the rectum into the posterior vaginal wall.
Q3. What is vault prolapse?
Answer: Descent of the vaginal apex following hysterectomy. It results from inadequate support of the vaginal apex and may coexist with anterior or posterior compartment prolapse.
Q4. What is the POP-Q system?

Answer: It is a standardised system for quantifying pelvic organ prolapse by measuring defined points of the vaginal walls and apex relative to the hymen during straining. It classifies prolapse from stage 0 to stage IV.
Q5. What are the risk factors for pelvic organ prolapse?

Answer: Increasing age, vaginal childbirth, pelvic floor injury, menopause-related tissue changes, obesity, chronic constipation, chronic cough, previous pelvic surgery and inherited connective tissue susceptibility.
Q6. What is the first-line treatment for mild symptomatic prolapse?

Answer: Conservative management, including supervised pelvic floor muscle training, lifestyle measures and consideration of a vaginal pessary. Treatment should be individualised to symptoms and preferences.
Q7. What is a vaginal pessary?

Answer: A removable device placed in the vagina to support prolapsed pelvic organs. It can relieve symptoms without surgery but requires appropriate fitting, follow-up and monitoring for complications.
Q8. Why is post-void residual urine measured?

Answer: To determine whether the bladder empties adequately. Significant residual urine may indicate impaired emptying or obstruction and can increase the risk of urinary infection and other complications.
Q9. Does every woman with prolapse require surgery?
Answer: No. Treatment is based on symptoms, impact on quality of life, associated complications and patient preference. Many women benefit from conservative management or a pessary.
Q10. What are the indications for surgery?

Answer: Persistent bothersome symptoms despite conservative treatment, patient preference for definitive treatment after counselling, or selected complications. The procedure depends on the compartment involved, health status and the patient's goals.
Q11. Can prolapse cause urinary incontinence?

Answer: Yes. Prolapse may coexist with stress or urgency urinary incontinence. In some patients, significant prolapse can mask stress incontinence by altering urethral position, so continence assessment may be important before surgery.
Q12. What symptoms suggest a rectocele?
Answer: A posterior vaginal bulge, constipation, incomplete bowel evacuation and the need to press on the vagina or perineum to facilitate defecation.
Calling every prolapse a uterine prolapse.
Failing to assess the anterior, posterior and apical compartments separately.
Forgetting to ask about urinary retention, incontinence and bowel symptoms.
Staging prolapse without adequate examination or measurements.
Assuming the anatomical stage directly determines treatment.
Recommending surgery before discussing conservative options.
Forgetting to explain pessary follow-up and potential complications.
Missing exposed vaginal tissue ulceration or suspicious lesions.
Ordering routine imaging when the clinical diagnosis is straightforward.
Failing to consider the patient's sexual function, goals and treatment preferences.
Cystocele and other anterior compartment prolapse.
Rectocele and enterocele.
Uterine, cervical or vaginal vault prolapse.
C — Conservative measures and pelvic floor muscle training.
A — Assess associated bladder, bowel and sexual symptoms.
R — Ring or other appropriate pessary; review regularly.
E — Evaluate surgical options according to symptoms and patient preference.
